title: Théorie des cycles algébriques : conjectures de Hodge, Tate, Lefschetz, Weil : notes manuscrites (s.d.), lettre (1965).

deep.reconstruction:
This page sets out an axiomatic framework for algebraic cycles on abelian varieties, in the spirit of the standard-conjectures material in this folder.

(1) Setting. Let VA be the additive category of abelian varieties over an algebraically closed field k. A word after 'définie' is crossed out; it may be 'à l'isogénie près', but the integral coefficients used below suggest Grothendieck works integrally. The category carries two structures:
- A duality functor *: VA° → VA, A ↦ A* (the dual abelian variety).
- A contravariant functor C*: VA° → (graded commutative rings in degrees ≥ 0 with C^0 ≅ Z), A ↦ C*(A), the ring of cycles modulo algebraic equivalence with intersection product.
- A dimension function that is additive (dim A×B = dim A + dim B) and invariant under duality (dim A* = dim A).

(2) Top and bottom degrees. If n = dim A, then C^n(A) ≅ Z via the degree of 0-cycles. This isomorphism is canonical but not functorial: pullback multiplies the top class by the degree of the map, so it is not natural for the contravariant structure. By contrast, C^0(A) ≅ Z is functorial (the fundamental class).

Grothendieck then adds a covariant law (proper pushforward) for cycles, together with the projection formula f_*(f^*x · y) = x · f_*y, which he says contains the formula for transposition of correspondences. He remarks that one can then derive 'formally' the Pontryagin product law on cycles, x*y = m_*(p_1^*x · p_2^*y) for the addition map m: A×A → A. The machine reading 'Pythagore' should be 'Pontrjagin'.

(3) The 'fundamental map'. He writes C^1(A) → Hom(A,A*)^alt, factored through C^1(A×A). The factorization is L ↦ m^*L − p_1^*L − p_2^*L, i.e. Mumford's Λ(L), followed by the theorem of divisorial correspondences:
C^1(A×B) / (p_1^*C^1(A) + p_2^*C^1(B)) ≅ Hom(A, B*).
The composite is NS(A) → Hom(A,A*), L ↦ φ_L. Its image is the symmetric homomorphisms, equivalently the alternating (Riemann / Weil-pairing) forms; this is what 'alt' refers to.

The boxed N.B. says that one could define A* axiomatically by this formula: A* is the object representing divisorial correspondences, Hom(B, A*) ≅ DivCorr(B, A). The final line 'au choix' presumably means one may take either the duality or the cycle structure as primitive.

Purpose: an axiomatic package (duality, cycle ring, pushforward, projection formula, Pontryagin product, divisor-class/homomorphism dictionary). It is presumably meant for formal arguments toward Lefschetz/Hodge-type statements (positivity, Rosati) for abelian varieties. The page is an outline only; nothing is proved here.
errors: Notation 'C^1(A)×C^1(B)' in the quotient should be the subgroup p_1^*C^1(A) + p_2^*C^1(B) of C^1(A×B) (a direct sum); this is harmless shorthand.

'Hom(A,A*)^alt': in modern conventions the image of NS(A) is the symmetric homomorphisms (φ̂ = φ). 'Alternating' is correct only after translating into Riemann forms or the Weil pairing e^L. This is a convention matter, not a real error.
Whether C^n(A) ≅ Z is 'functorial' depends on the variance: degree is compatible with pushforward but not with pullback. The note is correct for the contravariant C*.

ideas.what: Category of abelian varieties with duality functor and contravariant graded cycle ring (cycles mod algebraic equivalence) as axiomatic structure
ideas.modern_name: Cycle theory / Chow rings of abelian varieties with dual abelian variety; precursor of axiomatic Weil-cohomology-style frameworks
ideas.usually_credited_to: Weil, Lang, Mumford (Abelian Varieties, 1970); axiomatics in the spirit of Grothendieck's standard conjectures
ideas.where_published: Related only in spirit: Grothendieck, 'Standard conjectures on algebraic cycles' (1969)

ideas.what: Covariant pushforward plus projection formula implying transposition and the Pontryagin product
ideas.modern_name: Pushforward/projection formula; Pontryagin product on Chow groups of abelian varieties
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Fulton; Beauville 1983 for the Pontryagin-product structure on Chow groups)

ideas.what: NS(A) → C^1(A×A) → Hom(A,A*) via m^*L − p_1^*L − p_2^*L, and C^1(A×B)/(p_1^*+p_2^*) ≅ Hom(A,B*)
ideas.modern_name: Theorem of the square / map φ_L; theorem of divisorial correspondences (NS(A×B) = NS(A)⊕NS(B)⊕Hom(A,B^))
ideas.where_published: Related only in spirit: duality of abelian schemes via Picard schemes in FGA (Grothendieck, Bourbaki seminar on the Picard scheme)

ideas.what: Defining the dual A* axiomatically as the object representing divisorial correspondences
ideas.modern_name: Dual abelian variety as representing object of DivCorr / Pic^0

missed.claim: The axiomatic package here contains all ingredients of the Fourier transform on cycles of abelian varieties: duality, a cycle ring with pushforward, the Pontryagin product, and C^1(A×B) ↔ Hom(A,B*), which supplies the Poincaré class in C^1(A×A*). The Fourier transform itself (Mukai 1981; Beauville 1983 on Chow groups) is not mentioned. This is a suggestive but implicit proximity, not an explicit anticipation.
missed.quote: On peut en tirer formellement la loi de Pontrjagin pour les cycles ... N.B. On pourrait définir axiomatiquement A* par cette formule
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Shows Grothendieck was formalising the structure (A, A*, intersection and Pontryagin products) on which Beauville's decomposition and Fourier duality later rest. It is of historical interest only.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a sketch of standard facts about abelian varieties (duality, NS(A) → Hom(A,A^), divisorial correspondences, Pontryagin product) organised axiomatically. The axiomatic, category-level framing and the remark about defining A* by representability are mildly interesting historically. Nothing here is new mathematics.
transcription_corrections: 'loi de Pythagore[?]' should read 'loi de Pontrjagin' (Pontryagin product on cycles).
The crossed-out phrase after 'catégorie (additive) définie' is uncertain. It may be 'à l'isogénie près' (crossed out), followed by 'sur un corps alg. clos k'.
'C^n(A) ⇄ Z isom can, mais pas fonctoriel' is followed by a marginal '∃ / pas isom.' that seems to qualify the arrows (an isomorphism exists, but it is not natural).
In the quotient, 'C^1(A×B)/C^1(A)×C^1(B)' is written above the vertical '≀' linking it to 'C^1(A×B) → Hom(A,B*)'.
The final line 'au au choix' is probably 'ou au choix' (either option may be taken as primitive).
